## Introduction

In a recent episode of the [Software Engineering
Radio](https://www.se-radio.net/) podcast, I interviewed [Jeroen
Janssens](https://jeroenjanssens.com/), the Head of Developer Relations at
Posit, and [Thijs Nieuwdorp](https://thijsnieuwdorp.com/), a Developer
Relations Engineer at [Polars](https://pola.rs/). Our conversation focused on
Polars, a data frame library whose core is implemented in Rust and which offers
bindings for Python, R, and Node.js. Jeroen and Thijs also wrote [Python
Polars: The Definitive Guide](https://polarsguide.com/), the book that anchored
our discussion of expressions, joins, concatenation, and performance. This
episode was a joy to record --- I hope you appreciate it!

## Insights

I'm thankful that both Jeroen and Thijs took the time for this interview!
Before you listen to the full episode, please check out some of its insights:

**What makes Polars fast and why do developers keep using it?**

Jeroen explains the origin story of Polars and what attracts developers to it:

> "Now, about five years ago, Ritchie was trying to join two tables for some
> client work that he had to do, and he just was not satisfied with how slow
> Pandas were for that task. So, Ritchie being Ritchie, he tried to implement
> this himself using Rust. ... And now fast forward five years, we have this
> incredibly fast library with an expressive API for working with data. ...
> Now within the community, we often say that you come for the speed, but you
> stay for the API when it comes to Polars."

**What does it mean that Polars can process data that is "out of core"?**

Thijs describes the streaming engine that allows Polars to work with data sets
that are too large for memory:

> "So “out of core” indicates a set of algorithms that is designed to process
> data that are too large to fit into a computer's main memory all at once. And
> what the streaming engine does is it chops the data up in parts and process
> it as far as it can go, generally reducing peak memory usage. And of course,
> depending on the circumstances like the dataset and the query, oftentimes you
> can process datasets that are larger than RAM."

**What is an expression, and why is it the foundation of the Polars API?**

Jeroen explains why expressions deserve so much of your attention:

> "Yes, expressions are small things, but they are vital to Polars itself. ...
> And I think it's safe to say that when you understand expressions, you've
> mastered over 80% of the API that Polars offers and it's a big API. So, think
> of expressions as small operations that you can stack together to create a
> full query and chaining them, meaning adding a method to an existing object,
> right? Method chaining as Python programmers are very fond of as opposed to
> when you're working in R which is more functional."

He also offers the precise definition that he and Thijs settled on for the
book:

> "An expression is a tree of operations that describe how to construct one or
> more series."

**How does the query optimizer make a Polars pipeline faster?**

Jeroen describes why a lazy query can beat the equivalent eager code:

> "Now the query optimizer then looks at that blueprint to find the fastest
> path to your result. It uses several tricks. One is called predicate push
> down, and it moves your filters as close to the data source as possible. It
> also uses a projection push down. So, the engine only reads the specific
> columns you actually need for your analysis. ... Now lazy mode is a bit
> smarter because it waits until the very end to run everything."

The switch to that lazy mode is a small change, since you only need to scan
your data instead of reading it:

> "you have to make sure that you start off in lazy mode by either using a scan
> function instead of a read function, right? If you were to, for example, use
> read_CSV, you read the entire CSV file into memory, when you do scan_CSV, it
> will start off in lazy mode and again, only read the parts that are actually
> necessary."

**How much faster is Polars when a real production pipeline is migrated?**

Thijs tells the story of porting a utilities pipeline from Pandas to Polars,
starting with a single, deliberately modest piece of it:

> "I took one part of the pipeline's, relatively straightforward, it is like 30
> seconds of runtime, and it was just, okay, grab data frame out of the Cloud,
> added it to the existing data and then applied some business rules. So, in
> pandas that took about 30 seconds and then I transferred that to Polars, and
> we got it down to 1.2 seconds ... what originally would've cost about 150,000
> for the entire calculation. We brought that down to 3.5 K euros, which is
> well under the budgeted 5K Euro. So, a total reduction in cost of 98%."

Jeroen adds an important lesson for anyone who wants to repeat this migration
in their own code base:

> "you cannot do this on a line-by-line basis because the two are just so
> different."
